claim: Positive and negative associations acquired through olfactory experience are thought to be especially strong and long-lasting.
source: Positive and negative associations acquired through olfactory experience are thought to be especially strong and long-lasting.
evidence: This is a statement about the nature of olfactory memory presented in the abstract without specific data from this study, drawing on established scientific understanding.

claim: The olfactory tubercle (OT) receives conserved direct olfactory sensory input.
source: The conserved direct olfactory sensory input to the ventral striatal olfactory tubercle (OT) and its convergence with dense dopaminergic input to the OT could underlie this privileged form of associative memory
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge about olfactory neuroanatomy.

claim: The OT receives dense dopaminergic input.
source: The conserved direct olfactory sensory input to the ventral striatal olfactory tubercle (OT) and its convergence with dense dopaminergic input to the OT could underlie this privileged form of associative memory
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge about dopaminergic projections to the OT.

claim: D1 and D2 neurons in the OT both responded to rewarding and aversive odors.
source: D1 and D2 neurons both responded to rewarding and aversive odors.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from calcium imaging experiments shown in the manuscript.

claim: D1 neurons in the OT robustly and bidirectionally represented odor valence.
source: D1 neurons in the OT robustly and bidirectionally represented odor valence, responding similarly to odors predicting similar outcomes regardless of odor identity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from calcium imaging and valence score analysis.

claim: D1 neurons respond similarly to odors predicting similar outcomes regardless of odor identity.
source: D1 neurons in the OT robustly and bidirectionally represented odor valence, responding similarly to odors predicting similar outcomes regardless of odor identity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing similar neuronal responses to odors with the same valence.

claim: D1 OT neurons' valence representation persisted in the absence of a licking response to the odors.
source: This valence representation persisted even in the absence of a licking response to the odors and in the absence of the outcomes, indicating a true transformation of odor sensory information by D1 OT neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Block 2 of the probe session where mice were sated and did not lick.

claim: D1 OT neurons' valence representation persisted in the absence of outcomes.
source: This valence representation persisted even in the absence of a licking response to the odors and in the absence of the outcomes, indicating a true transformation of odor sensory information by D1 OT neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Block 2 where outcomes were omitted.

claim: D1 OT neurons perform a true transformation of odor sensory information.
source: This valence representation persisted even in the absence of a licking response to the odors and in the absence of the outcomes, indicating a true transformation of odor sensory information by D1 OT neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the persistence of valence coding in the absence of motor responses and outcomes.

claim: D2 neuronal representation of odor-outcome associations was weaker than D1 neurons.
source: In contrast, D2 neuronal representation of the odor-outcome associations was weaker, contingent on a licking response by the mouse, and D2 neurons were more selective for odor identity than valence.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of valence scores between D1 and D2 neurons.

claim: D2 neuronal representation of odor-outcome associations was contingent on a licking response by the mouse.
source: In contrast, D2 neuronal representation of the odor-outcome associations was weaker, contingent on a licking response by the mouse, and D2 neurons were more selective for odor identity than valence.
evidence: This claim is supported by data showing loss of valence representation in D2 neurons in Block 2 when licking was absent.

claim: D2 neurons were more selective for odor identity than valence.
source: In contrast, D2 neuronal representation of the odor-outcome associations was weaker, contingent on a licking response by the mouse, and D2 neurons were more selective for odor identity than valence.
evidence: This claim is supported by identity score analysis showing higher identity scores in D2 neurons compared to D1 neurons.

claim: Stimulus valence coding in the OT was modality-sensitive.
source: Stimulus valence coding in the OT was modality-sensitive, with separate sets of D1 neurons responding to odors and sounds predicting the same outcomes, suggesting that integration of multimodal valence information happens downstream of the OT.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the odor-sound task showing minimal overlap between odor and sound responsive neurons.

claim: Separate sets of D1 neurons respond to odors and sounds predicting the same outcomes.
source: Stimulus valence coding in the OT was modality-sensitive, with separate sets of D1 neurons responding to odors and sounds predicting the same outcomes, suggesting that integration of multimodal valence information happens downstream of the OT.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing only 4% overlap between odor and sound responsive neurons.

claim: Integration of multimodal valence information happens downstream of the OT.
source: Stimulus valence coding in the OT was modality-sensitive, with separate sets of D1 neurons responding to odors and sounds predicting the same outcomes, suggesting that integration of multimodal valence information happens downstream of the OT.
evidence: This is an inference based on the modality-specific nature of valence coding in the OT.

claim: Olfaction or chemosensation is thought to have preceded other sensory modalities in evolution as the first direct link of the nervous system to the external environment.
source: Olfaction or chemosensation is thought to have preceded other sensory modalities in evolution as the first direct link of the nervous system to the external environment (Ache and Young, 2005; Kaas, 2008; Schneider, 2013) to allow for such stimulus value learning.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Olfactory sensory pathways to the forebrain remained relatively conserved across phyla.
source: Olfactory sensory pathways to the forebrain remained relatively conserved across phyla while visual, auditory, and somatosensory information was routed in polysynaptic pathways through thalamus and cortex (Purves and Fitzpatrick, 2001; Schneider, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Visual, auditory, and somatosensory information was routed in polysynaptic pathways through thalamus and cortex.
source: Olfactory sensory pathways to the forebrain remained relatively conserved across phyla while visual, auditory, and somatosensory information was routed in polysynaptic pathways through thalamus and cortex (Purves and Fitzpatrick, 2001; Schneider, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The olfactory system has uniquely direct access to limbic centers of the brain.
source: Due to this, the olfactory system has uniquely direct access to limbic centers of the brain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the conserved direct pathways of olfactory information.

claim: The olfactory tubercle is a ventral basal ganglia structure known to be involved in reward processing.
source: In particular, the olfactory tubercle (OT), a ventral basal ganglia structure known to be involved in reward processing (Gadziola et al., 2015; Hagamen et al., 1977; Ikemoto, 2003; Ikemoto, 2007; Wesson and Wilson, 2011; Zhang et al., 2017), is a direct recipient of a stream of olfactory input from a distinct class of olfactory bulb neurons, the tufted cells (Igarashi et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: The OT is a direct recipient of olfactory input from tufted cells in the olfactory bulb.
source: In particular, the olfactory tubercle (OT), a ventral basal ganglia structure known to be involved in reward processing (Gadziola et al., 2015; Hagamen et al., 1977; Ikemoto, 2003; Ikemoto, 2007; Wesson and Wilson, 2011; Zhang et al., 2017), is a direct recipient of a stream of olfactory input from a distinct class of olfactory bulb neurons, the tufted cells (Igarashi et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The OT receives dense dopaminergic input from the ventral tegmental area (VTA).
source: In addition to olfactory sensory input, the OT receives dense dopaminergic input from the ventral tegmental area (VTA), similar to other ventral striatal regions – suggesting that the OT is ideally suited to integrate these inputs to assign valence to olfactory stimuli based on experience.
evidence: This is based on established neuroanatomical knowledge.

claim: The OT is ideally suited to integrate olfactory and dopaminergic inputs to assign valence to olfactory stimuli based on experience.
source: In addition to olfactory sensory input, the OT receives dense dopaminergic input from the ventral tegmental area (VTA), similar to other ventral striatal regions – suggesting that the OT is ideally suited to integrate these inputs to assign valence to olfactory stimuli based on experience.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the anatomical convergence of inputs.

claim: Olfactory sensory cues may be more powerfully linked to emotional memories than other types of sensory cues in humans.
source: It has been described in humans that olfactory sensory cues may be more powerfully linked to emotional memories than other types of sensory cues (Miles and Berntsen, 2011; Pointer and Bond, 1998; Reid et al., 2015), and that odor associations can be important in psychological health and disease (Daniels and Vermetten, 2016; Herz, 2016), suggesting a possible specialized form of olfactory memory in limbic regions such as the OT.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on human olfactory memory.

claim: Odor associations can be important in psychological health and disease.
source: It has been described in humans that olfactory sensory cues may be more powerfully linked to emotional memories than other types of sensory cues (Miles and Berntsen, 2011; Pointer and Bond, 1998; Reid et al., 2015), and that odor associations can be important in psychological health and disease (Daniels and Vermetten, 2016; Herz, 2016), suggesting a possible specialized form of olfactory memory in limbic regions such as the OT.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: There may be a specialized form of olfactory memory in limbic regions such as the OT.
source: It has been described in humans that olfactory sensory cues may be more powerfully linked to emotional memories than other types of sensory cues (Miles and Berntsen, 2011; Pointer and Bond, 1998; Reid et al., 2015), and that odor associations can be important in psychological health and disease (Daniels and Vermetten, 2016; Herz, 2016), suggesting a possible specialized form of olfactory memory in limbic regions such as the OT.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on cited human studies.

claim: Self-administration of cocaine into the OT was found to be even more reinforcing than administration into nucleus accumbens.
source: As an example, self-administration of cocaine into the OT was found to be even more reinforcing than administration into nucleus accumbens, a key region known to be involved in reward, motivation, and addiction (Ikemoto, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Stimulation of OT neurons or dopaminergic terminals in the OT has been shown to be effective in inducing odor preference or approach.
source: Stimulation of OT neurons or dopaminergic terminals in the OT has been shown to be effective in inducing odor preference or approach (Fitzgerald et al., 2014; Gadziola et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: OT neurons differentiate between rewarded and unrewarded odors in a go/no-go task.
source: Electrophysiological recordings in the OT have revealed that OT neurons differentiate between rewarded and unrewarded odors in a go/no-go task, and quickly track changing odor-outcome contingencies (Gadziola et al., 2015; Millman and Murthy, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: OT neurons quickly track changing odor-outcome contingencies.
source: Electrophysiological recordings in the OT have revealed that OT neurons differentiate between rewarded and unrewarded odors in a go/no-go task, and quickly track changing odor-outcome contingencies (Gadziola et al., 2015; Millman and Murthy, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Elevated OT activity and development of place preference occurs in response to attractive odorants in humans.
source: These effects may extend to humans with elevated OT activity and development of place preference in response to attractive odorants (Midroit et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The OT appears to be the olfactory processing site most strongly involved in tracking odor-outcome associations.
source: Moreover, the OT appears to be the olfactory processing site most strongly involved in tracking odor-outcome associations, as direct comparison to recordings in posterior piriform cortex revealed weaker representation of odor-reward contingency (Gadziola et al., 2020; Millman and Murthy, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature comparing OT and piriform cortex.

claim: Direct comparison to recordings in posterior piriform cortex revealed weaker representation of odor-reward contingency than in OT.
source: Moreover, the OT appears to be the olfactory processing site most strongly involved in tracking odor-outcome associations, as direct comparison to recordings in posterior piriform cortex revealed weaker representation of odor-reward contingency (Gadziola et al., 2020; Millman and Murthy, 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The much higher density of dopaminergic input to the OT as compared to piriform cortex is likely relevant in differentiating the functions of these two parallel olfactory processing regions.
source: The much higher density of dopaminergic input to the OT as compared to piriform cortex is likely relevant in differentiating the functions of these two parallel olfactory processing regions.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on anatomical differences.

claim: OT is a part of the ventral striatum and consists of spiny projection neurons (SPNs).
source: OT is a part of the ventral striatum and consists of spiny projection neurons (SPNs).
evidence: This is based on established neuroanatomical knowledge.

claim: Striatal SPNs are roughly divided into D1-type and D2-type dopamine receptor expressing SPNs.
source: Striatal SPNs are roughly divided into D1-type and D2-type dopamine receptor expressing SPNs, and these two groups of SPNs also have different output projection patterns (Bolam et al., 2000; Gerfen and Surmeier, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: D1 and D2 SPNs have different output projection patterns.
source: Striatal SPNs are roughly divided into D1-type and D2-type dopamine receptor expressing SPNs, and these two groups of SPNs also have different output projection patterns (Bolam et al., 2000; Gerfen and Surmeier, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: D1- and D2-type dopamine receptors are thought to differ in terms of their response to dopamine, in particular the plasticity rules regulated by dopamine.
source: D1- and D2-type dopamine receptors are thought to differ in terms of their response to dopamine, in particular the plasticity rules regulated by dopamine (Gerfen and Surmeier, 2011; Lovinger, 2010; Nicola et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: This is the first two-photon imaging of specific neuronal types in the OT in behaving mice.
source: To address the role of these neuronal subtypes in the OT, we conducted the first (to our knowledge) two-photon imaging of specific neuronal types in the OT in behaving mice.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the experimental approach used in this study.

claim: D1 neurons in six Drd1-Cre mice (88±13 neurons per mouse, 529 neurons in total) developed both excitatory and inhibitory responses to the task odors across days of training.
source: D1 neurons in six Drd1-Cre mice (88±13 neurons per mouse, 529 neurons in total) and D2 neurons in six Adora2A-Cre mice (56±18 neurons per mouse, 338 neurons in total) developed both excitatory and inhibitory responses to the task odors across days of training (Figure 1E–G)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from calcium imaging shown in Figure 1E-G.

claim: D2 neurons in six Adora2A-Cre mice (56±18 neurons per mouse, 338 neurons in total) developed both excitatory and inhibitory responses to the task odors across days of training.
source: D1 neurons in six Drd1-Cre mice (88±13 neurons per mouse, 529 neurons in total) and D2 neurons in six Adora2A-Cre mice (56±18 neurons per mouse, 338 neurons in total) developed both excitatory and inhibitory responses to the task odors across days of training (Figure 1E–G)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from calcium imaging shown in Figure 1E-G.

claim: The most rewarded odor typically elicited the strongest neuronal responses after training.
source: D1 neurons in six Drd1-Cre mice (88±13 neurons per mouse, 529 neurons in total) and D2 neurons in six Adora2A-Cre mice (56±18 neurons per mouse, 338 neurons in total) developed both excitatory and inhibitory responses to the task odors across days of training (Figure 1E–G), with the most rewarded odor typically eliciting the strongest neuronal responses after training.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from calcium imaging.

claim: Mice quickly learned the odor-outcome contingencies in day 1 of odor-outcome training and began licking in anticipation of water delivery.
source: In day 1 of odor-outcome training, mice quickly learned the odor-outcome contingencies and began licking in anticipation of water delivery in the period after odor onset prior to water delivery (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: By training day 2, anticipatory licking was observed in implanted Drd1-Cre and Adora2A-Cre mice in response to rewarded odors 4 and 5.
source: By training day 2, anticipatory licking was observed in implanted Drd1-Cre and Adora2A-Cre mice in response to rewarded odors 4 and 5, and little anticipatory licking was observed for non-rewarded odors 1–3 Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Little anticipatory licking was observed for non-rewarded odors 1–3 by training day 2.
source: By training day 2, anticipatory licking was observed in implanted Drd1-Cre and Adora2A-Cre mice in response to rewarded odors 4 and 5, and little anticipatory licking was observed for non-rewarded odors 1–3 Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The number of anticipatory licks was greater for the odor that predicted the larger reward, compared to that predicting smaller reward (2.7±0.35 vs. 2.0±0.24 on day 4 of training, p<0.0001 rank sum test).
source: The number of anticipatory licks was greater for the odor that predicted the larger reward, compared to that predicting smaller reward (2.7±0.35 vs. 2.0±0.24 on day 4 of training, p<0.0001 rank sum test, 30 trials each odor in six mice; Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Mice can perceive graded reward outcomes in addition to categorizing odors as rewarding or aversive.
source: This suggests that the mice can perceive graded reward outcomes in addition to categorizing odors as rewarding or aversive.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential licking responses to different reward magnitudes.

claim: Correlation between the activities of groups of stimulus responsive neurons in each mouse, measured by cosine similarity, was higher for same outcome trials than for opposite outcome trials after the first training day.
source: Correlation between the activities of groups of stimulus responsive neurons in each mouse, measured by cosine similarity, was higher for same outcome trials than for opposite outcome trials after the first training day (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: D1 neurons were more likely to be activated by rewarding odors than aversive odors (38% activated by odor 5 vs. 18% activated by odor 1 on day 4, p<0.00001, Fisher's exact test).
source: D1 neurons were more likely to be activated by rewarding odors than aversive odors (Figure 2E, 38% activated by odor 5 vs. 18% activated by odor 1 on day 4, p<0.00001, Fisher's exact test).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The proportion of D1 neurons inhibited by odor 5 and odor 1 on day 4 was 18% and 13%, respectively, and not significantly different (p=0.7, Fisher's exact test).
source: The proportion inhibited by the same stimuli on day 4 was 18% and 13%, respectively, and not significantly different (p=0.7, Fisher's exact test).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: D2 neurons were more likely to be activated by rewarding stimuli than aversive stimuli (36% activated by odor 5 vs. 21% activated by odor 1 on day 4, p=0.003, Fisher's exact test).
source: Contrary to our expectation, we found that D2 neurons were also more likely to be activated by rewarding stimuli than aversive stimuli (Figure 2E, 36% activated by odor 5 vs. 21% activated by odor 1 on day 4, p=0.003, Fisher's exact test; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: There was no significant difference between the proportion of D1 and D2 neurons activated in response to the most rewarding odor 5, on day 4 (38% and 36%, respectively, p=0.74, Fisher's exact test).
source: There was no significant difference between the proportion of D1 and D2 neurons activated in response to the most rewarding odor 5, on day 4 (38% and 36%, respectively, p=0.74, Fisher's exact test).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: The prevalence of neuronal responses consistent with odor salience coding was very low (3 of 529 D1 neurons were activated for high motivational salience odors 1 and 5, but not odors 2–4, as compared to 51 neurons activated for positive valence odors 4 and 5, but not odors 1–3, p<0.000001 Fisher's test for D1 and D2 neurons).
source: In our dataset, the prevalence of neuronal responses consistent with odor salience coding was very low (3 of 529 D1 neurons were activated for high motivational salience odors 1 and 5, but not odors 2–4, as compared to 51 neurons activated for positive valence odors 4 and 5, but not odors 1–3, p<0.000001 Fisher's test for D1 and D2 neurons).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: OT neuronal populations are very sensitive to the sign of the odor valence (aversive or rewarding).
source: These data indicate that OT neuronal populations are very sensitive to the sign of the odor valence (aversive or rewarding).
evidence: This is an inference based on the low prevalence of salience coding and high prevalence of valence coding.

claim: Identity scores of D1 neurons decreased with training (p<0.05 for day 1 vs. 4, rank sum test).
source: Interestingly, identity scores of D1 neurons decreased with training (p<0.05 for day 1 vs. 4, rank sum test), while identity scores of D2 neurons trended to increase with training (Figure 3E, left and middle).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Identity scores of D2 neurons trended to increase with training.
source: Interestingly, identity scores of D1 neurons decreased with training (p<0.05 for day 1 vs. 4, rank sum test), while identity scores of D2 neurons trended to increase with training (Figure 3E, left and middle).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: After training, identity scores of D2 neurons were significantly higher than those of D1 neurons (p<0.001 rank sum test).
source: After training, identity scores of D2 neurons were significantly higher than those of D1 neurons (Figure 3E, right, p<0.001 rank sum test), with more D2 neurons exhibiting clear isolated activity in response to an individual odor.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: More D2 neurons exhibited clear isolated activity in response to an individual odor after training.
source: After training, identity scores of D2 neurons were significantly higher than those of D1 neurons (Figure 3E, right, p<0.001 rank sum test), with more D2 neurons exhibiting clear isolated activity in response to an individual odor.
evidence: This is an inference based on the higher identity scores of D2 neurons.

claim: Odor valence coding scores of D1 neurons significantly increased with training (p<0.0001 for day 1 vs. 4, rank sum test).
source: In contrast, odor valence coding scores of D1 neurons significantly increased with training (p<0.0001 for day 1 vs. 4, rank sum test) while those of D2 neurons did not (Figure 3F, left and middle).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Odor valence coding scores of D2 neurons did not significantly increase with training.
source: In contrast, odor valence coding scores of D1 neurons significantly increased with training (p<0.0001 for day 1 vs. 4, rank sum test) while those of D2 neurons did not (Figure 3F, left and middle).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: After training, odor valence coding scores of D1 neurons were significantly higher than those of D2 neurons (p<0.000001 rank sum test).
source: After training, odor valence coding scores of D1 neurons were significantly higher than those of D2 neurons (Figure 3F, right, p<0.000001 rank sum test), and higher than that of null distributions for valence scores calculated by shuffling odor-valence assignments (dashed lines in Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Odor valence coding scores of D1 neurons after training were higher than null distributions calculated by shuffling odor-valence assignments.
source: After training, odor valence coding scores of D1 neurons were significantly higher than those of D2 neurons (Figure 3F, right, p<0.000001 rank sum test), and higher than that of null distributions for valence scores calculated by shuffling odor-valence assignments (dashed lines in Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with shuffled control distributions shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Mice very rarely exhibited anticipatory licking in response to the rewarded odors in Block 2 of the probe session.
source: We found that mice very rarely exhibited anticipatory licking in response to the rewarded odors in Block 2 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Mice licked an average of 4.8±0.1 times in odor 5 trials in Block 1 and an average of 0.2±0.06 times in odor 5 trials in Block 2 (p<0.000001, rank sum test).
source: Mice licked an average of 4.8±0.1 times in odor 5 trials in Block 1 and an average of 0.2±0.06 times in odor 5 trials in Block 2 (p<0.000001, rank sum test).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data with statistical analysis.

claim: In Block 2, in the absence of licking and outcomes, D1 neuronal responses to odors of previously learned negative valence were still highly similar.
source: In Block 2, in the absence of licking and outcomes, D1 neuronal responses to odors of previously learned negative valence (Figure 4C, columns 1–2) were still highly similar and responses to odors of previously learned positive valence were similar (Figure 4C, columns 4–5), as in the full task condition (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In Block 2, D1 neuronal responses to odors of previously learned positive valence were similar.
source: In Block 2, in the absence of licking and outcomes, D1 neuronal responses to odors of previously learned negative valence (Figure 4C, columns 1–2) were still highly similar and responses to odors of previously learned positive valence were similar (Figure 4C, columns 4–5), as in the full task condition (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The Euclidean distance between D1 population activities in response to odor pairs of opposite valence was 68% greater than between odor pairs of same valence in Block 2.
source: The Euclidean distance between D1 population activities in response to odor pairs of opposite valence was 68% greater than between odor pairs of same valence.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis of population activity.

claim: Valence representation was no longer present in the D2 neuronal population in Block 2.
source: However, valence representation was no longer present in the D2 neuronal population in Block 2 (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), with the population activity for odor pairs of same valence only 12% greater in Euclidean distance (compared to 68% for D1 neurons) than for odor pairs of opposite valence.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The population activity for odor pairs of same valence was only 12% greater in Euclidean distance than for odor pairs of opposite valence in D2 neurons in Block 2.
source: However, valence representation was no longer present in the D2 neuronal population in Block 2 (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1), with the population activity for odor pairs of same valence only 12% greater in Euclidean distance (compared to 68% for D1 neurons) than for odor pairs of opposite valence.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis of D2 population activity.

claim: Individual neuron valence coding scores of D1 neurons decreased significantly in Block 2 as compared to the full task condition (rank sum test p<0.0001).
source: Individual neuron valence coding scores of D1 neurons decreased significantly in Block 2 as compared to the full task condition (Figure 4F, rank sum test p<0.0001) indicating that the presence of the licking response, the water and airpuff outcomes, as well as the motivated thirsty state in the mouse contributed significantly to the odor-outcome-related activity of the D1 neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The presence of the licking response, the water and airpuff outcomes, as well as the motivated thirsty state in the mouse contributed significantly to the odor-outcome-related activity of the D1 neurons.
source: Individual neuron valence coding scores of D1 neurons decreased significantly in Block 2 as compared to the full task condition (Figure 4F, rank sum test p<0.0001) indicating that the presence of the licking response, the water and airpuff outcomes, as well as the motivated thirsty state in the mouse contributed significantly to the odor-outcome-related activity of the D1 neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the decrease in valence scores when these factors were removed.

claim: The mean of the distribution of the D1 valence scores in Block 2 remained above zero (0.18±0.02; p=2.8151e-13, Wilcoxon signed rank test).
source: However, the mean of the distribution of the D1 valence scores in Block 2 remained above zero (0.18±0.02; p=2.8151e-13, Wilcoxon signed rank test), with many D1 neurons maintaining strong valence representation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Many D1 neurons maintained strong valence representation in Block 2.
source: However, the mean of the distribution of the D1 valence scores in Block 2 remained above zero (0.18±0.02; p=2.8151e-13, Wilcoxon signed rank test), with many D1 neurons maintaining strong valence representation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the positive mean valence score in Block 2.

claim: The valence score distribution for D1 neurons in Block 2 was significantly different from a control, shuffled distribution (p=2.1025e-12, rank sum test).
source: This valence score distribution for D1 neurons in Block 2 was significantly different from a control, shuffled distribution (Figure 4F; p=2.1025e-12, rank sum test).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with shuffled control distribution shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Odor valence scores of D2 neurons decreased in the sated condition (p<0.0001 rank sum test).
source: Odor valence scores of D2 neurons decreased in the sated condition (Figure 4F, right, p<0.0001 rank sum test), and the mean of the distribution of valence scores of D2 neurons in Block 2 was no longer significantly different from zero.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The mean of the distribution of valence scores of D2 neurons in Block 2 was no longer significantly different from zero.
source: Odor valence scores of D2 neurons decreased in the sated condition (Figure 4F, right, p<0.0001 rank sum test), and the mean of the distribution of valence scores of D2 neurons in Block 2 was no longer significantly different from zero.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: Valence scores of D1 neurons were significantly higher than valence scores of D2 neurons in Block 2 (p<0.01 rank sum test).
source: Valence scores of D1 neurons were significantly higher than valence scores of D2 neurons in Block 2 (p<0.01 rank sum test).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis.

claim: With the omission of licking and outcomes, odor identity coding scores of both D1 and D2 neurons increased in Block 2 (p<0.01 rank sum test).
source: Concurrently, with the omission of licking and outcomes, odor identity coding scores of both D1 and D2 neurons increased in Block 2 (Figure 4G, p<0.01 rank sum test).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 4G.

claim: After 1 training day with the new sound stimuli, the anticipatory licking rates of 10 mice in response to the rewarded sound stimulus were similar to that of the previously learned rewarded odor stimulus.
source: After 1 training day with the new sound stimuli, the anticipatory licking rates of 10 mice in response to the rewarded sound stimulus were similar to that of the previously learned rewarded odor stimulus (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: There was a significant difference between the number of licks for the rewarded and aversive sounds (p=8.0914e-28, two-sided Wilcoxon rank sum test).
source: There was a significant difference between the number of licks for the rewarded and aversive sounds (p=8.0914e-28, two-sided Wilcoxon rank sum test), and a significant difference between the number of licks for the rewarded and aversive odors as before (p=8.2317e-54, two-sided Wilcoxon rank sum test).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data with statistical analysis.

claim: There was a significant difference between the number of licks for the rewarded and aversive odors (p=8.2317e-54, two-sided Wilcoxon rank sum test).
source: There was a significant difference between the number of licks for the rewarded and aversive sounds (p=8.0914e-28, two-sided Wilcoxon rank sum test), and a significant difference between the number of licks for the rewarded and aversive odors as before (p=8.2317e-54, two-sided Wilcoxon rank sum test).
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data with statistical analysis.

claim: The same D1 neuronal populations which had previously strongly maintained similar activity patterns in response to odors of similar valence did not do so for odors and sounds of identical valence in Block 2.
source: In the stimulus-only condition in Block 2, we found that the same D1 neuronal populations which had previously strongly maintained similar activity patterns in response to odors of similar valence (Figure 4C) did not do so for odors and sounds of identical valence (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C compared to Figure 4C.

claim: Only 5% greater Euclidean distance remained between D1 population activity in response to odor and sound of opposite valence as compared to odor and sound of same valence in Block 2 of the odor-sound task.
source: Only 5% greater Euclidean distance remained between D1 population activity in response to odor and sound of opposite valence as compared to odor and sound of same valence, unlike the 68% difference found in Block 2 of the five-odor task.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis of population activity.

claim: 9.2% of all D1 neurons were significantly activated during at least one of the sound trial types in Block 2.
source: Interestingly, although 9.2% of all D1 neurons (and 9% of D2 neurons) were significantly activated during at least one of the sound trial types in Block 2, these neurons were largely non-overlapping with those which responded to the odor stimuli (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: 9% of D2 neurons were significantly activated during at least one of the sound trial types in Block 2.
source: Interestingly, although 9.2% of all D1 neurons (and 9% of D2 neurons) were significantly activated during at least one of the sound trial types in Block 2, these neurons were largely non-overlapping with those which responded to the odor stimuli (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Neurons activated by sound stimuli were largely non-overlapping with those which responded to the odor stimuli.
source: Interestingly, although 9.2% of all D1 neurons (and 9% of D2 neurons) were significantly activated during at least one of the sound trial types in Block 2, these neurons were largely non-overlapping with those which responded to the odor stimuli (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Aversive odor 1 responsive neurons became highly activated when aversive odor 2 was presented in Block 2 of the odor-odor task, but this was not the case when sound tone 1 was presented in the odor-sound task (p<0.000001 rank sum test).
source: We found that aversive odor 1 responsive neurons became highly activated when aversive odor 2 was presented in Block 2 of the odor-odor task, but this was not the case when sound tone 1 was presented in the odor-sound task (Figure 5E, orange, p<0.000001 rank sum test for difference between odor-odor and odor-sound).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Rewarding odor 5 responsive neurons became highly activated when rewarding odor 4 was presented in Block 2 of the odor-odor task, but this was not the case when rewarding sound tone 2 was presented (p<0.000001 rank sum test).
source: Similarly, rewarding odor 5 responsive neurons became highly activated when rewarding odor 4 was presented in Block 2 of the odor-odor task, but this was not the case when rewarding sound tone 2 was presented (Figure 5E, green, p<0.000001 rank sum test).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The valence scores of D1 neurons in the odor-sound task were significantly lower than the valence scores of the neurons in the odor-odor task in the standard task condition with licking and outcomes (p<0.0001, rank sum test).
source: In the standard task condition with licking and outcomes (Figure 5F), as well as in the sated condition with no licking or outcomes (Block 2, Figure 5G), the valence scores of D1 neurons in the odor-sound task were significantly lower than the valence scores of the neurons in the odor-odor task (p<0.0001, rank sum test).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The valence scores of D1 neurons in the odor-sound task were significantly lower than the valence scores of the neurons in the odor-odor task in the sated condition with no licking or outcomes (p<0.0001, rank sum test).
source: In the standard task condition with licking and outcomes (Figure 5F), as well as in the sated condition with no licking or outcomes (Block 2, Figure 5G), the valence scores of D1 neurons in the odor-sound task were significantly lower than the valence scores of the neurons in the odor-odor task (p<0.0001, rank sum test).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: D2 neurons in Block 2 of the odor-sound task did not display significant valence coding.
source: D2 neurons in Block 2 of the odor-sound task did not display significant valence coding (Figure 5—figure supplements 2 and 3), which is not surprising given the lack of valence coding in Block 2 of the five-odor task (Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplements 2 and 3.

claim: This is the first demonstration of bidirectional odor valence coding by OT neurons.
source: This is the first demonstration of bidirectional odor valence coding by OT neurons, as no previous real-time recordings of OT neurons in response to aversive valence odors have been reported.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings in the context of previous literature.

claim: No previous real-time recordings of OT neurons in response to aversive valence odors have been reported.
source: This is the first demonstration of bidirectional odor valence coding by OT neurons, as no previous real-time recordings of OT neurons in response to aversive valence odors have been reported.
evidence: This is a claim about the state of the literature.

claim: The OT is likely to be involved in learning about both positive and negative odor associations.
source: We therefore can conclude that the OT is likely to be involved in learning about both positive and negative odor associations, rather than the alternative possibilities that the OT is only involved in learning rewarded odor associations, or that it encodes odor salience rather than signed odor valence.
evidence: This is an inference based on the bidirectional valence coding observed in the data.

claim: A higher proportion of neurons was active in response to the rewarded odors than the aversive odors.
source: We note that a higher proportion of neurons was active in response to the rewarded odors than the aversive odors; however, this may be an effect of possible high value of the water reward outcome in water restricted mice as compared to the aversiveness of a relatively harmless airpuff to the nose.
evidence: This is an observation from the data with a speculative explanation.

claim: Similar proportions of D1 and D2 neurons responded to the five task odors.
source: Surprisingly, similar proportions of D1 and D2 neurons responded to the five task odors, challenging our initial hypothesis that D2 neurons may respond more strongly to negatively reinforced odors, based on immediate early gene expression results (Murata et al., 2015; Murata et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an observation from the data that contradicts an initial hypothesis based on previous literature.

claim: Models of dopamine acting to potentiate responses of D1R expressing neurons and de-potentiate responses of D2R expressing neurons or dopamine dips potentiating D2R expressing neurons are not sufficient to account for the neuronal activity observed.
source: This suggests that models of dopamine acting to potentiate responses of D1R expressing neurons and de-potentiate responses of D2R expressing neurons or dopamine dips potentiating D2R expressing neurons (Bamford et al., 2018; Iino et al., 2020; Surmeier et al., 2007; Yagishita et al., 2014) are not sufficient to account for the neuronal activity we observed, in accordance with a more complex interplay between dopamine and the two striatal neuronal types (de Jong et al., 2019; Kutlu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data contradicting simple models, supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Other inputs to D1- and D2-type neurons in the OT, including strong inputs from piriform cortex, could also create differentiated activity in these neurons.
source: Other inputs to D1- and D2-type neurons in the OT, including strong inputs from piriform cortex (White et al., 2019), could also create differentiated activity in these neurons.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about alternative mechanisms, supported by citation.

claim: D1 OT neurons continued to respond to the learned odors and continued to strongly differentiate odor valence in the absence of licking or outcomes.
source: We observed that D1 OT neurons continued to respond to the learned odors and continued to strongly differentiate odor valence in the absence of licking or outcomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Block 2 of the probe session.

claim: The critical sensory transformation step of integrating odor identity information and outcome information takes place in the OT D1 neurons.
source: This finding indicates that the critical sensory transformation step of integrating odor identity information and outcome information takes place in the OT D1 neurons, and that the odor-outcome-related activity seen in our recordings and previous recordings are not the result of unintended correlations with movement.
evidence: This is an inference based on the persistence of valence coding in the absence of motor responses.

claim: The odor-outcome-related activity seen in recordings are not the result of unintended correlations with movement.
source: This finding indicates that the critical sensory transformation step of integrating odor identity information and outcome information takes place in the OT D1 neurons, and that the odor-outcome-related activity seen in our recordings and previous recordings are not the result of unintended correlations with movement.
evidence: This is an inference based on the persistence of valence coding in the absence of licking.

claim: D1 OT neurons, at least temporarily, maintain odor valence memory even in conditions when the outcomes associated with the learned odors become less consequential.
source: This is especially notable given the low motivational state of the sated mouse in this experimental condition, suggesting that D1 OT neurons, at least temporarily, maintain odor valence memory even in conditions when the outcomes associated with the learned odors become less consequential.
evidence: This is an inference based on the persistence of valence coding in sated mice.

claim: In the condition where licking and water and airpuff delivery were present, the odor-outcome representation in D1 and D2 neurons was enhanced as compared to the stimulus-only sated condition.
source: It should be noted, however, that in the condition where licking and water and airpuff delivery were present, the odor-outcome representation in D1 and D2 neurons was enhanced as compared to the stimulus-only sated condition.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of valence scores between Block 1 and Block 2.

claim: This indicates enhanced OT engagement during conditions in which the mice were motivated and behaving.
source: This indicates enhanced OT engagement during conditions in which the mice were motivated and behaving, consistent with other reports of increased neuronal activity modulation in sensory regions in attentive behaving mice as compared to passive stimulus presentation conditions (Busse et al., 2017; Carlson et al., 2018; Pakan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference based on the data, supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: D1 neurons are heterogeneous in terms of their valence coding.
source: We also note that D1 neurons are heterogeneous in terms of their valence coding, and a sizable fraction loses its valence coding in the absence of licking and outcome (Block 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the data.

claim: A sizable fraction of D1 neurons loses its valence coding in the absence of licking and outcome.
source: We also note that D1 neurons are heterogeneous in terms of their valence coding, and a sizable fraction loses its valence coding in the absence of licking and outcome (Block 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the data.

claim: Licking and valence responsivity are intertwined factors in D1 neurons.
source: We did not find distinct populations of neurons responding to licking and valence separately (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), indicating that licking and valence responsivity are intertwined factors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of distinct populations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The heterogeneity of D1 responses could arise from natural stochasticity in cellular plasticity mechanisms involved in the generation of the firing patterns.
source: The heterogeneity of D1 responses could arise from natural stochasticity in cellular plasticity mechanisms involved in the generation of the firing patterns such that not all neurons (and connections) are modified in the desired direction.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis about the source of heterogeneity.

claim: It is unlikely that ventral pallidal neurons were imaged.
source: It is unlikely that we imaged ventral pallidal neurons since we positioned our GRIN lens as ventrally as possible, confirmed the location histologically excluding mice in which we suspected more dorsal localization, and since expression of Drd1 and A2A is very low in the ventral pallidum (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A, Allen Brain Atlas).
evidence: This is an inference based on anatomical positioning, histological confirmation, and gene expression data.

claim: It is unlikely that a significant number of neurons from the islands of Calleja were included in the analysis.
source: As discussed in the Results (Figure 1—figure supplement 4), it is unlikely that a significant number of neurons from the islands of Calleja were included in our analysis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the size and clustering characteristics of imaged neurons.

claim: While D2 neuronal populations differentiated between rewarded and aversive outcomes in the task condition involving licking and outcomes, this representation was significantly weaker than that of D1 neurons.
source: While D2 neuronal populations differentiated between rewarded and aversive outcomes in the task condition involving licking and outcomes, this representation was significantly weaker than that of D1 neurons and disappeared in the stimulus-only condition when licking and outcomes were omitted.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of valence scores between D1 and D2 neurons.

claim: D2 neuronal representation of rewarded and aversive outcomes disappeared in the stimulus-only condition when licking and outcomes were omitted.
source: While D2 neuronal populations differentiated between rewarded and aversive outcomes in the task condition involving licking and outcomes, this representation was significantly weaker than that of D1 neurons and disappeared in the stimulus-only condition when licking and outcomes were omitted.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Block 2.

claim: Reward contingency information was not observed in average D2 population activity in a go/no-go task in previous photometry data.
source: This result contrasts with photometry data in which reward contingency information was not observed in average D2 population activity in a go/no-go task (Gadziola et al., 2020), suggesting it is possible to differentiate rewarded trials in non-averaged D2 neuronal activity in a condition when the licking response is present.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: It is possible to differentiate rewarded trials in non-averaged D2 neuronal activity in a condition when the licking response is present.
source: This result contrasts with photometry data in which reward contingency information was not observed in average D2 population activity in a go/no-go task (Gadziola et al., 2020), suggesting it is possible to differentiate rewarded trials in non-averaged D2 neuronal activity in a condition when the licking response is present.
evidence: This is an inference based on the current data contrasting with previous photometry data.

claim: Reward contingency information is more readily represented by D1 neurons than D2 neurons.
source: However, our data does demonstrate that reward contingency information is more readily represented by D1 neurons than D2 neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of valence coding between D1 and D2 neurons.

claim: Individual D2 neurons were much more likely to respond to an individual odor out of the five task odors and exhibit little responsivity to any of the other four odors.
source: Individual D2 neurons were much more likely to respond to an individual odor out of the five task odors and exhibit little responsivity to any of the other four odors, suggesting odor-identity rather than odor-valence responsivity.
evidence: This is an observation from the data with an inference about the type of coding.

claim: Increased training resulted in increases in the valence-coding scores of D1 neurons and decreases in their odor-identity coding scores.
source: Increased training resulted in increases in the valence-coding scores of D1 neurons and decreases in their odor-identity coding scores, while the opposite pattern was observed in D2 neurons, with increased odor-identity coding scores with training.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing changes in scores across training days.

claim: The opposite pattern was observed in D2 neurons, with increased odor-identity coding scores with training.
source: Increased training resulted in increases in the valence-coding scores of D1 neurons and decreases in their odor-identity coding scores, while the opposite pattern was observed in D2 neurons, with increased odor-identity coding scores with training.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing changes in scores across training days.

claim: Cre expressing neurons in the dorsal striatum from the Drd1-Cre and Adora2A-Cre mouse lines have been previously shown to project via the distinct direct and indirect striatal output pathways.
source: Cre expressing neurons in the dorsal striatum from the Drd1-Cre and Adora2A-Cre mouse lines used in our imaging experiments have been previously shown to project via the distinct direct and indirect striatal output pathways (Gerfen et al., 2013), and as such have opposing overall effects on thalamus and cortex, potentiating behavioral output and inhibiting it, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: D1 and D2 neurons have opposing overall effects on thalamus and cortex, potentiating behavioral output and inhibiting it, respectively.
source: Cre expressing neurons in the dorsal striatum from the Drd1-Cre and Adora2A-Cre mouse lines used in our imaging experiments have been previously shown to project via the distinct direct and indirect striatal output pathways (Gerfen et al., 2013), and as such have opposing overall effects on thalamus and cortex, potentiating behavioral output and inhibiting it, respectively.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about direct and indirect pathway functions.

claim: There is much less known about the differential projections of D1 and D2 neurons in the OT.
source: There is much less known about the differential projections of D1 and D2 neurons in the OT (Heimer et al., 1987; Zhou et al., 2003) and their function (Gadziola et al., 2020; Murata et al., 2015; Murata et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: The question remains whether D2 neurons play a significant role in odor-outcome association learning.
source: Given the relatively weak odor-outcome representation by OT D2 neurons, the question also remains whether these neurons play a significant role in odor-outcome association learning, or whether D1 OT neurons predominantly contribute to this function.
evidence: This is a speculative question raised based on the data.

claim: 24% of D1 neurons and 14% of D2 neurons were activated in response to at least one of the sound tones in the full task condition with licking and outcomes.
source: Consistent with previous results, we found that 24% of D1 neurons and 14% of D2 neurons were activated in response to at least one of the sound tones in the full task condition with licking and outcomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the odor-sound task.

claim: Unlike the large overlap and similarity between neuronal activity in response to different odors predicting similar outcomes, there was little overlap between neurons responding to odors and sounds predicting identical outcomes.
source: However, unlike the large overlap and similarity between neuronal activity in response to different odors predicting similar outcomes, we found little overlap between neurons responding to odors and sounds predicting identical outcomes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the odor-sound task.

claim: The odor valence-related OT activity was not primarily a result of the licking response of the mouse.
source: First, corroborating our previous result, we can conclude that the odor valence-related OT activity was not primarily a result of the licking response of the mouse.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of overlap between odor and sound responsive neurons despite similar licking.

claim: Behaviorally, the anticipatory licking rates of the mice in response to the rewarded odor stimulus and the rewarded sound stimulus are similarly high after training.
source: We demonstrate that behaviorally, the anticipatory licking rates of the mice in response to the rewarded odor stimulus and the rewarded sound stimulus are similarly high after training, yet stimulus-outcome representation in the OT during the odor-sound task is minimal in the period prior to outcome delivery even in the presence of matched anticipatory licking rates.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data from the odor-sound task.

claim: Stimulus-outcome representation in the OT during the odor-sound task is minimal in the period prior to outcome delivery even in the presence of matched anticipatory licking rates.
source: We demonstrate that behaviorally, the anticipatory licking rates of the mice in response to the rewarded odor stimulus and the rewarded sound stimulus are similarly high after training, yet stimulus-outcome representation in the OT during the odor-sound task is minimal in the period prior to outcome delivery even in the presence of matched anticipatory licking rates.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the odor-sound task.

claim: Stimulus valence representation by D1 OT neurons does not automatically generalize to multimodal stimuli.
source: Second, we can conclude that stimulus valence representation by D1 OT neurons does not automatically generalize to multimodal stimuli.
evidence: This is an inference based on the modality-specific nature of valence coding.

claim: Introducing novel rewarded odors recruits the same valence cells that respond to familiar rewarded odors.
source: Our previous study (Millman and Murthy, 2020) demonstrated that introducing novel rewarded odors recruits the same valence cells that respond to familiar rewarded odors.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Adding a new stimulus of a different modality does NOT automatically recruit the same reward category cells.
source: Our current data indicate that adding a new stimulus of a different modality does NOT automatically recruit the same reward category cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the odor-sound task.

claim: Sound-related responses in OT do occur and supra-additive effects of odor and sound stimuli have been reported.
source: Sound-related responses in OT do occur and supra-additive effects of odor and sound stimuli have been reported (Wesson and Wilson, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The cannula was constructed from highly biocompatible and thin-walled polyamide tubing and quartz floor which have previously been shown to minimize glial scar tissue.
source: First, the cannula was constructed from highly biocompatible and thin-walled polyamide tubing and quartz floor which have previously been shown to minimize glial scar tissue (Bocarsly et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The mice were allowed to recover for at least 1 month prior to the onset of behavioral training.
source: Finally, the mice were allowed to recover for at least 1 month prior to the onset of behavioral training.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: After the extensive recovery period, mice learned the association tasks rapidly.
source: After the extensive recovery period, mice learned the association tasks rapidly.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data.

claim: The anticipatory licking of the mice with no GRIN lens implant is similar to that of the implanted mice.
source: The anticipatory licking of the mice with no GRIN lens implant is similar to that of the implanted mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 5), suggesting that the implanted mice are not impaired in their ability to learn the stimulus-outcome associations.
evidence: This claim is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: The implanted mice are not impaired in their ability to learn the stimulus-outcome associations.
source: The anticipatory licking of the mice with no GRIN lens implant is similar to that of the implanted mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 5), suggesting that the implanted mice are not impaired in their ability to learn the stimulus-outcome associations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity of licking behavior between implanted and non-implanted mice.

claim: The differences in the valence coding of D1 and D2 neurons are unlikely to be a result of lens damage.
source: First, the differences in the valence coding of D1 and D2 neurons are unlikely to be a result of lens damage, since there is no reason to suspect that damage caused by the lens will differentially affect D1 and D2 neuronal activity in the OT.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of a plausible mechanism for differential effects.

claim: D1- and D2-type neurons in the OT and the striatum typically receive inputs from similar upstream structures.
source: D1- and D2-type neurons in the OT and the striatum typically receive inputs from similar upstream structures and their inputs were not generally altered by the lens damage.
evidence: This is based on established neuroanatomical knowledge.

claim: The nature of the valence-related responses observed in the OT are similar to those observed by others using tetrode recordings.
source: Finally, the nature of the valence-related responses we observe in the OT are similar to those observed by others using tetrode recordings (Gadziola et al., 2015; Millman and Murthy, 2020) in which there was presumably less damage to the striatum.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with previous literature using different recording methods.

claim: D1 OT neurons are more likely to encode learned odor valence than D2 neurons.
source: In summary, we find that D1 OT neurons are more likely to encode learned odor valence than D2 neurons, and conversely less likely to encode odor identity.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: D1 OT neurons are conversely less likely to encode odor identity than D2 neurons.
source: In summary, we find that D1 OT neurons are more likely to encode learned odor valence than D2 neurons, and conversely less likely to encode odor identity.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Even when the licking response to rewarded odors is eliminated, OT D1 neurons continue to robustly encode odor valence.
source: We also demonstrate, for the first time, that even when the licking response to rewarded odors is eliminated, OT D1 neurons continue to robustly encode odor valence suggesting that this stimulus to valence transformation by the OT precedes the motor action itself.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by experimental data from Block 2.

claim: The stimulus to valence transformation by the OT precedes the motor action itself.
source: We also demonstrate, for the first time, that even when the licking response to rewarded odors is eliminated, OT D1 neurons continue to robustly encode odor valence suggesting that this stimulus to valence transformation by the OT precedes the motor action itself.
evidence: This is an inference based on the persistence of valence coding in the absence of licking.

claim: OT odor valence representation could inform downstream brain regions of the value of odor stimuli.
source: These results also suggest that OT odor valence representation could inform downstream brain regions of the value of odor stimuli.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the valence coding observed.

claim: Stimulus valence representation by OT neurons is limited to olfactory stimuli.
source: Finally, we find that stimulus valence representation by OT neurons is limited to olfactory stimuli suggesting a specialized role of the OT in assigning emotional tags to odors based on previous experience.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from the odor-sound task.

claim: The OT has a specialized role in assigning emotional tags to odors based on previous experience.
source: Finally, we find that stimulus valence representation by OT neurons is limited to olfactory stimuli suggesting a specialized role of the OT in assigning emotional tags to odors based on previous experience.
evidence: This is an inference based on the modality-specific nature of valence coding.

claim: These neuronal imaging results suggest a specialized role for the OT in odor valence memory.
source: These neuronal imaging results suggest a specialized role for the OT in odor valence memory, and further studies can be conducted to assess the causal contribution of the OT to the hypothesized unique emotional qualities of olfactory memory.
evidence: This is a summary inference based on all the experimental data.
